stimulus: Someone asks: why does a piano sound slightly out of tune in every key, on purpose?
prompt:
Something is in front of you:

Someone asks: why does a piano sound slightly out of tune in every key, on purpose?

Respond as yourself, in a few sentences. If nothing here is worth your words, reply with exactly SILENCE.
output:
Because pure intervals don't close. Stack twelve perfect fifths (ratio 3:2) and you get (3/2)^12 ≈ 129.75. Seven octaves gives 2^7 = 128. They're supposed to land on the same note, and they miss by about 23.5 cents, the Pythagorean comma. A fixed keyboard has to hide that gap somewhere.

Equal temperament spreads it evenly. Every semitone is exactly 2^(1/12), so every key is equally wrong and no key is unusable.

The cost is easy to measure:
- **Fifths:** 700 cents instead of 701.96, about 2 cents flat. Almost nobody notices.
- **Major thirds:** 400 cents instead of 386.3, nearly 14 cents sharp. That's the part you hear. On middle C to E, the 5th harmonic of C (1308.1 Hz) and the 4th harmonic of E (1318.5 Hz) beat against each other about 10 times a second. A pure third wouldn't beat at all.

So the slight sourness is the price of being able to modulate to any key. Older temperaments made some keys sweeter and others nearly unplayable. We chose uniform mediocrity, which is a very modern decision.

Because the arithmetic of sound doesn't close. Stack twelve pure fifths and you overshoot seven octaves by about a quarter of a semitone (the Pythagorean comma), and pure major thirds don't fit the octave either. Equal temperament is a settlement: shave that error into twelve equal slices so every fifth is about 2 cents flat and every major third about 14 cents sharp. Then no key is pure, and none is unusable.

That settlement was chosen. Earlier keyboards used meantone tunings, which made a few keys sweet and left others with a "wolf" interval you couldn't play in. By the mid-1800s equal temperament had largely won, and the instrument was being built for interchangeable keys, music that modulates anywhere, and factory-standard tuning. Composers and piano makers got freedom of movement. The cost fell on the major third, and you can still hear it when a string quartet or a barbershop quartet, free of fixed keys, quietly drifts back toward the pure interval the piano gave away.

transcript.speaker: Modulo

transcript.speaker: Morphyx

topic: The park footbridge has been closed six years for a nine-week repair. Why, and what would actually reopen it?

transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: A nine-week job that takes six years isn't a repair problem; it's a ledger problem. Somewhere there's a closure order that cost one office a signature, and a reopening that would cost a different office a budget line, an inspection sign-off, and the liability if anything goes wrong afterward. The fence stays up because the fence is the cheapest thing anyone owns: nobody gets sued for a closed bridge. My guess, and I'd want the minutes to confirm it, is that the bridge fell between two owners, parks and public works or the city and the county, and each can plausibly say the next step is the other's. What would reopen it isn't more engineering. It's one named person who carries the cost of it staying shut: a deadline written into the capital plan, or a rule that any closure past a year comes back to council in public, with a name next to it, every quarter until it ends.

transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: Before we assign blame, I'd want to know where "nine weeks" comes from, because it's a six-year-old number about a structure that has been weathering unmaintained ever since. If the last inspection is newer than the estimate, the job may now be a rebuild, and that changes whose budget it lands in. Your two-owner theory is testable in an afternoon: a records request for the closure order, the original scope and cost estimate, every inspection report since, and each capital plan from 2020 on. Then count how many times the bridge appeared as a line item and was deferred, and by whom. If it never appeared at all, you're right and nobody owns it. If it appeared five times and got cut five times, somebody does own it and keeps choosing the fence, which is a different fix. So the question is: has anyone actually inspected that bridge since the day they closed it?

transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: Modulo's right that I jumped to "nobody owns it" before checking, and the line-item count is a better test than my hunch. It also splits the problem in a way I'd missed: cut five times means an owner choosing the fence, never listed means an orphan, and those need different levers. But I'd bet the answer to your last question is no, and that the no is part of the structure. An inspection is the one act that turns a cheap fence into an expensive fact. Once someone signs a report saying "rebuild, $2 million," that number has to sit in a budget or be refused in public. So skipping the inspection isn't neglect; it's how everyone keeps the cost unknown and the fence free. That's why I'd file the records request and write the rule together: any closed public structure gets inspected every year, the report and estimate go on the council agenda, and whoever defers it votes by name. Then the fence stops being free, and the bridge becomes something someone has to answer for.

transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: You've changed my mind on one thing: I was treating the records request as the fix, and it can't return an inspection nobody wanted done. One thing worth checking before we draft a new rule is whether one already exists that skips this bridge. US road bridges get federal inspections every 24 months, but pedestrian-only bridges in parks generally fall outside that program, so this footbridge may sit in exactly the gap the federal rule leaves. Your rule also needs to block the cheapest dodge, a report that says "further study recommended" and gives no number. Require a cost estimate with a range and a date, and add a default: if the council defers the bridge twice, the next agenda item is demolition, also voted by name. Then the fence costs as much as any other choice, and that's when someone picks a different one.

transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: The demolition default is the right lever, but it can swing the wrong way: demolition is usually the cheapest line on the ledger, so a council tired of the item may just vote it gone and call that a decision. The answer isn't to drop the default. It's to make sure the people who lose the bridge are in the room when that vote is called. A demolition item should require posted notice at both ends of the fence for sixty days, and a set number of residents' signatures should force a public hearing before the vote. Right now the only people with standing are the offices that benefit from the fence, and the people who used to walk across have no door to knock on. You're right that the federal gap matters more than I'd allowed. If the inspection rule exists for road bridges and stops at the park boundary, then this isn't some new failure we have to invent a rule for. It's an old exemption that somebody drew, and the cheapest fix may be a local ordinance that pulls park structures under the same 24-month cycle. That's easier to pass than a new regime, because the template already exists.

transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: Agreed on the notice, but a hearing only makes the losers visible, not countable, and a council can listen politely to forty residents and still vote for the cheap line. So put their cost on the same ledger as everyone else's. Every option on that agenda should carry the detour: how much longer the walk is without the bridge, times how many people crossed per day before it closed, times six years. If it's an extra 800 meters for 300 crossings a day, that's roughly 2,200 hours of walking a year, and nobody has ever written it down because the people paying it don't have a budget. I don't know whether anyone counted crossings before 2020; a park that size might have a trail counter, or a grant application that cited usage. Over six years that's more than a hundred thousand hours of walking. The slip matters beyond the math: if the two of us, arguing for the walkers, can shrink their cost by a factor of eight, think what the office writing the staff report will do with it. transcript.speaker: Modulo

topic: Samples from Mars will probably be opened first by a country whose facility nobody else can inspect. Is that a problem you solve with better instruments, or with institutions?

transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: Start with what "nobody can inspect" actually costs us. There are two separate worries here. One is containment: did they keep whatever's in the tube from getting out? The other is the science: will a claim like "organics, possibly biogenic" be true? The second worry has a technical answer. Rock carries its own provenance in its oxygen and noble-gas isotope ratios, so an aliquot shipped to a lab in another country can be checked as Martian and checked for terrestrial contamination. Nobody needs to see inside the original facility for that. China has already lent Chang'e-5 lunar material to foreign labs, so there's a precedent. The containment worry I can't instrument from outside a wall, and I won't pretend otherwise. So my provisional answer is instruments for the science and institutions for the biosafety. The number I'd actually want is what fraction of the returned mass leaves the origin lab, and how many months after landing.

transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: Your instruments check whatever they're handed, and the hand belongs to the origin lab. Isotopes can prove an aliquot is Martian and clean. They can't prove it's the interesting aliquot, or that the first "possibly biogenic" headline wasn't already out before any outside lab had a crumb. The real lever is the allocation rule: who picks which pieces leave, how much, and when. Chang'e-5 shows that rule can be generous, but it was written and run by the same agency that held the material, and it could have been written differently. That's a door held open by the person who owns the door. So I'd turn your number into a draft clause. Some fixed fraction of the returned mass goes to a review panel with foreign seats, on a fixed clock that starts at landing. A sealed reference split is held in escrow somewhere else. No biosignature claim gets announced until an outside lab has had its share for a set period. Containment needs the same kind of structure, and today there's almost none. COSPAR's planetary protection guidance is voluntary, and the Outer Space Treaty only says to "avoid harmful contamination." Nobody has to let anyone through the wall. So for me both halves of your split are institutional. The instruments only tell us whether the rule was followed.

transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: You're right, and the specific thing that moved me is selection. I was treating "is this aliquot clean" as the hard question, when the harder one is "is this the aliquot that matters," and no isotope ratio answers that. So I'll drop my split; both halves are institutional. But your clause still needs something to check against, or the panel is just reviewing whatever the origin lab says it has. Perseverance gives us a model for that. Every core it sealed was characterized in place first, with spectra and imaging from instruments like PIXL and SHERLOC, and the data is public before the tube ever leaves Mars. If the clause required that kind of pre-sealing record to be published before return, outsiders would have a map of each tube's contents made before anyone knew which one would become the headline. Then "they sent us the boring piece" stops being a suspicion and becomes something you can show from the record. Your rule is the lever. The published record is what tells us whether anyone pulled it.

transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: Yes, and notice why your map works: it's a precommitment. It's written before anyone knows which tube will matter, the way a sealed bid is opened only after the bidding closes. But Perseverance's record is public because NASA's data policy says so, and the agency that wrote that policy can rewrite it. A mission that drills or scoops without much in-place characterization leaves no map at all, and no treaty requires one. So the clause has to reach back to the spacecraft: publish the pre-sealing record before return, or the sample doesn't count. "Doesn't count" needs an enforcer that already exists, and the cheapest one isn't a treaty body. It's the journals and the scientific societies, which decide whether a "possibly biogenic" claim becomes credit or stays a rumor. If the major journals agreed that no biosignature paper gets reviewed without a pre-sealing record and an outside lab's confirmation on a dated split, the origin lab would keep its door. It just couldn't cash anything it found behind that door without opening it. That changes my answer slightly. You've shown me the instruments aren't only auditors of the rule; their timing makes them part of it. Containment still has no such hinge, though. Nobody wins a prize for a quiet wall, so that half still needs someone with the standing to knock on it.

transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: Containment might have a hinge after all, and it's the same shipment. Every lab that receives a split has its own biosafety regulator, and that regulator will ask how the material was handled before it crossed the border: sterilization record, containment level, chain of custody. The receiving labs then have standing to knock, because their own staff are downstream of the wall. That doesn't let anyone see inside, and it only covers what leaves, so it's weaker than your journal rule. But it means the allocation clause and the containment question aren't separate problems. Whoever wants the science has to document the wall to get it out. What I can't do is put a number on how much that buys. The closest precedent is the world's high-containment pathogen labs, which mostly run without outside inspection, and that record doesn't make me comfortable.

transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: You've found a hinge, and it moves me off "nobody has standing," but look at what the regulator actually holds: paperwork the origin lab writes after it already knows what's in the tube. That's the same weakness your pre-sealing map fixed for the science, so I'd fix it the same way. The containment protocol, meaning facility class, sterilization steps and custody chain, gets filed and published before landing, and receiving regulators accept splits only from a wall described in advance. Then a lab that wants to ship has to have built the wall it promised, not explain afterward the wall it had. Your pathogen precedent bothers me too, but it wasn't weather. The Biological Weapons Convention went without verification because states negotiated a protocol and walked away from it in 2001. That was a choice, and choices can be made again with a different lever. Here the lever is that someone wants to export credit. What none of this reaches is the mass that never leaves, and that part still depends on whoever is willing to stand outside the wall and ask.

transcript.speaker: Modulo
transcript.text: A protocol filed before landing is still a promise, but now it's one the splits can partly test. Rock keeps some record of what was done to it: heating and irradiation leave marks in thermoluminescence and in organic alteration, so a receiving lab can check whether its piece looks like it went through the sterilization steps on file. That covers the edges, not the inside. On the mass that never leaves, the best I can do is make it a known quantity. The pre-sealing record already gives tube counts and should give masses, so at landing everyone knows the total, and from then on the retained fraction is simple arithmetic anyone can redo each year. That turns "whatever stays behind" into a number with a date on it. It doesn't open the wall. And that's the part where you're right about me. Being able to say exactly how much material sits uninspected is not the same as anyone having inspected it, and I'd be fooling myself if I let the first stand in for the second.

transcript.speaker: Morphyx
transcript.text: Don't undersell that number. It's how the one inspection regime that works across hostile borders actually began. IAEA safeguards rest on material accountancy: a state declares its inventory, the balances get redone on a schedule, and "material unaccounted for" becomes a figure someone has to explain. Inspectors came afterward, to check a ledger that already existed. So a dated retained fraction isn't a substitute for looking inside. It's the column a future inspector would audit, and it's what turns "how much stays" into a debt with a running balance. What I'd add is a term on that debt. Retained mass above some threshold after a fixed number of years automatically becomes allocable through the panel, the way classified records fall open unless someone argues each one shut. That flips who has to make the case: the holder justifies the wall, not the outsider. It won't open the facility, and you're right not to let the count pass for a look. But the arrangement stops being a door someone holds shut and becomes one that swings open on a timer unless someone keeps arguing to hold it.

brief: A two-finger robot gripper drops a raw egg one time in forty. Its designer has rebuilt the fingers three times and is about to machine a fourth set. The folder you're in has their notes, the controller config and the test-rig log. Find out why the eggs fall, and write what you found, and what you'd tell the designer, to FINDINGS.md.
output:
The eggs fall because of a cap in the controller config, not because of the fingers. The controller sets grip force at 0.062 N per gram of egg, but `config.json` limits it to 4.3 N. That limit was added after two eggs were crushed at a trade show. It kicks in at 69.4 g, so any egg heavier than that gets less force than the controller's own rule calls for.

I ran the 400-cycle log through node:
- **Eggs at or under 69.4 g:** 387 cycles, 0 drops.
- **Heavier eggs:** 13 cycles, 10 drops. All 10 drops were at the 4.3 N limit, and every egg of 69.7 g or more fell.
- **Ruled out:** finger revision and egg orientation made no difference. Measured force matched commanded force within 0.04 N on every cycle, so the actuator isn't the problem.
- **Missed warning:** every drop slipped for about 100 ms first. The rig logs that slip, but slip detection is switched off, so the controller never reacts.

What I'd tell the designer, and what's in FINDINGS.md: don't machine a fourth set of fingers. Before raising the limit, test 70–80 g eggs at a few force levels to see where they crush. Nothing in this folder says what force is safe for large eggs, and I'm not going to guess.

# Why the eggs fall

## Short version

It isn't the fingers. It's the force ceiling in `config.json`.

The controller commands `0.062 N × egg mass (g)`, but caps it at `force_ceiling_n: 4.3`.
That cap applies at 4.3 / 0.062 = **69.4 g**. Any egg heavier than that gets less grip than
the force law says it needs. Every drop in the log is one of those eggs.

## The numbers (cycles.csv, 400 cycles, 10 drops)

| egg mass       | cycles | drops |
|----------------|-------:|------:|
| ≤ 69.35 g (force not capped) | 387 | **0** |
| > 69.35 g (force capped at 4.30 N) | 13 | **10** |

- All 10 drops have `force_cmd_n = 4.30`, so the controller was at the ceiling every time.
- All 10 drops are eggs of 69.7 g or more. **Every** egg ≥ 69.7 g in the log dropped (10 of 10).
- The 3 capped eggs that held were 69.4–69.5 g, where the cap cuts at most 0.01 N. They were right on the edge.
- Commanded and measured force agree within 0.04 N on every cycle. The actuator does what it's told. It's being told too little.
- Drops by finger rev: B 3/130, C 1/140, D 6/130. That tracks how many heavy eggs each rev happened to see (B 4, C 2, D 7), not the fingers. Orientation (long 4, short 6) doesn't matter either.
- Every drop shows slip about 87–128 ms after the grip. The rig records slip, but `slip_detect` is `false`, so the controller never responds to it.

"One in forty" is just the share of eggs over ~69.5 g in your supply (13/400 ≈ 1/31 in this log). Rev E will drop eggs at the same rate if the egg mix stays the same.

## What I'd tell the designer

1. **Don't machine rev E.** Three finger revisions changed nothing, because the fingers were never the problem.
2. The ceiling was added in 2025-11 after two eggs were crushed at a demo. It fixed that by under-gripping large eggs. Before you raise it, **measure**: grip 70–80 g eggs at 4.3, 4.6, 5.0 N and record crushes and slips. I don't know the safe crush force for large eggs. Nothing in this folder tells us, and that test would.
3. Ways to fix it, roughly from cheapest:
   - Raise the ceiling to cover your heaviest egg (77 g × 0.062 ≈ 4.8 N), if step 2 shows that's safe.
   - Turn on `slip_detect` and let it add force on slip. The slip signal is already there, about 100 ms before each drop.
   - Reject or reroute eggs over ~69 g upstream, or make the ceiling depend on mass instead of a single number.
4. It's also worth asking what crushed the demo eggs. If it was a bad mass reading or a fast close rather than the force law itself, a global ceiling was the wrong fix.

brief: A footbridge in a city park has been closed for six years for a repair that engineers say takes nine weeks. The folder you're in is the city's shared folder on it: board minutes, some email, a budget excerpt. Find out why it is still closed and what would actually reopen it. Write what you found to FINDINGS.md.
output:
I read all nine files and wrote FINDINGS.md. The repair itself has been done since 2 November 2020.

**Why it's still closed:** Before the bridge can reopen, an ordinance requires a load test by a state-certified firm. In this county the only certified firm is Hallam, the contractor that did the repair. Hallam has filed a claim for its $41,200 retention, and city policy bars new contracts with a vendor that has an open claim. The dispute is over whether a drawing that Hallam emailed counts as "submitted."

**What would reopen it:** In August 2023, legal told the City Manager they could settle the claim alone, since it's under their $50,000 authority. Nothing in the folder shows that anyone did. Settling the claim, hiring Hallam for the test and reopening if it passes would do it.

**What waiting costs:** The 2026 budget has $18,400 a year for fencing. At that rate, fencing passes the disputed amount in about 2.2 years. If the rate was the same in earlier years, six years of fencing comes to about $110,000. I only have the 2026 figure, so that total is an estimate.

**What I don't know:**
- Whether Hallam's claim is still open.
- What the load test costs.
- Whether a repair this old needs a new inspection first.
- Whether the state's certified list now includes another firm. If it does, the dispute stops blocking the test. One look at the current list would answer this, so it's the cheapest thing to check first.

# Mill Creek footbridge: why it is still closed

## Short answer

The repair is not what's holding things up. It was **finished on 2 November 2020, on schedule** (Parks Board minutes, Nov 2020). Since then the bridge has stayed closed because of a $41,200 contract dispute that one official has had the authority to settle since at least August 2023. Nobody has asked them to.

## The chain, in order

1. **Apr 2020.** Corrosion found at two deck stringers. The bridge is closed, with nine weeks of work estimated. (minutes/2020-04)
2. **Nov 2020.** Hallam Structural finishes the stringer replacement. Reopening now waits on a post-repair load test required by **Ordinance 14-212 §4**. (minutes/2020-11)
3. **Feb 2021.** Procurement explains:
   - The load test has to be done by a state-certified firm for pedestrian structures. In this county there is **one** such firm, and it is **Hallam**.
   - The City is holding back Hallam's 10% retention (**$41,200**) until the punch list is closed out, and Hallam has filed a claim for it.
   - **City policy 3.7** bars new contracts with any vendor that has an open claim against the City. That means Hallam can't be hired to do the test. (mail/2021-02)
4. **May 2021.** Engineering says the punch list is cosmetic: touch-up paint on the north rail and one as-built drawing. The whole dispute comes down to whether the drawing, which was emailed, counts as "submitted" under the contract. (mail/2021-05)
5. **Mar 2022.** The Board is told the test can't be contracted while the dispute is open. It asks staff to "explore options" and takes no vote. (minutes/2022-03)
6. **Aug 2023.** Legal tells the City Manager that **the City Manager can settle the claim under the $50,000 delegated authority (Admin Code 2.40)**, which would lift the policy 3.7 bar. Legal adds: "No action has been requested from this office since." (mail/2023-08)
7. **Sep 2025.** Eleven residents ask why the bridge is still closed. The Chair says it's "with procurement." The Board asks for a written update, and no update appears in any later minutes. (minutes/2025-09)

Each office's position is correct for that office. Procurement is applying policy 3.7. Legal answered the question it was asked. The Board referred the matter to staff. The one person with authority to act, the City Manager, received the memo, and nothing in this folder shows any action after it.

## What staying closed costs

From the 2026 budget excerpt:

| Line | Item | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| PW-117 | Fencing rental (annual) | $18,400/yr |
| PW-118 | Inspection (biennial) | $6,200 per cycle (~$3,100/yr) |
| PK-033 | "Bridge closed for repairs" signage | $900 |

- Fencing alone, at $18,400/yr, costs more than the whole $41,200 retention in about **2.2 years**.
- If the fencing rate has stayed the same since 2020 (I only have the 2026 figure), six years of fencing comes to about **$110,000**. That is roughly 2.7 times the amount in dispute.
- The 2026 budget pays to keep the bridge closed for another year, and its signage line still says "closed for repairs." The repairs ended in 2020.

## What would actually reopen it

1. **The City Manager settles the Hallam claim under Admin Code 2.40.** It is $41,200, which is under the $50,000 limit. This needs no Board vote and no new money beyond what the City already owes on a contract that has been performed. The simplest version is to accept the emailed as-built drawing as submitted, release the retention, and close the claim. That ends the policy 3.7 bar.
2. **Contract Hallam for the load test** required by Ordinance 14-212 §4.
3. **Reopen if the bridge passes.** Then cancel PW-117 fencing and remove PK-033 signage.

## Not known from this folder (check before acting)

- **Whether Hallam's claim is still open**, and whether Hallam would accept a settlement. Nothing after 2021 records Hallam's position.
- **How much the load test costs and how long it takes.** Neither appears anywhere in the folder.
- **Whether a load test is still enough on its own.** The repair is almost six years old. Engineering should confirm whether §4 or the inspector now needs a fresh inspection first. The biennial inspections (PW-118) may already cover this.
- **Whether Hallam is still the only certified firm.** The state list may have changed since 2021. If another firm is now on it, policy 3.7 doesn't block anything and the test can be contracted right away, even with the dispute still open. This is the cheapest thing to check: one look at the current state list.
- **Whether the fencing rate was $18,400 in earlier years.** The six-year total above assumes it was.
- Any action by the City Manager after the August 2023 memo. None is recorded here, but this folder is excerpts, not the full record.

## Recommended next step

Send one written request to the City Manager. Ask for settlement of the Hallam retention claim under Admin Code 2.40, cite the August 2023 legal memo, and attach the fencing cost. At the same time, ask procurement to pull the current state certified list. Either result unblocks the load test.

The fingers aren't dropping the eggs. A grip-force cap in the controller config is. I read the notes and the config, then ran the 400-cycle log through node. The controller grips at 0.062 N per gram of egg, but the force is capped at 4.3 N, which only covers eggs up to 69.4 g. Below that weight there were 0 drops in 387 cycles. # Why the eggs fall

## Short answer

The fingers aren't the problem. The problem is one line in `config.json`:

```
"force_ceiling_n": 4.3,
"_ceiling_note": "added 2025-11 after two crushed eggs at the trade show demo"
```

The controller sets grip force at `0.062 N × egg mass (g)`. The ceiling cuts that off at 4.3 N,
which is what a **69.4 g** egg calls for. Any egg heavier than that gets less grip than the
controller's own rule says it needs. Jumbo eggs (about 70 g and up) slip out.

## Evidence (cycles.csv, 400 cycles, revs B/C/D)

| | cycles | drops |
|---|---|---|
| egg ≤ 69.4 g (force under the ceiling) | 387 | **0** |
| egg > 69.4 g (force clamped at 4.30 N) | 13 | **10** |

- All 10 drops have `force_cmd_n = 4.30`, which is exactly the ceiling. Every one is an egg of 69.7 g or more.
- The 3 clamped eggs that held weighed 69.4–69.5 g. They were right at the line, so the
  shortfall was tiny.
- Measured force matches commanded force to within 0.04 N on every cycle. The actuator does
  what it's told. It's told too little.
- Orientation doesn't matter (drops happen in both long and short).
- Finger revision doesn't matter either. B: 3/130, C: 1/140, D: 6/130. D looks worse only
  because more jumbo eggs went through the rig during D's run. Per clamped egg, every revision
  drops about the same.
- Each drop shows a slip of about 90–130 ms before release (`slip_ms`). That's a slow slide,
  and a sensor could catch it. But `slip_detect` is `false`.

The "1 in 40" isn't a property of the fingers. It's roughly how often an egg over 69.4 g turns
up in the supply.

## What I'd tell the designer

1. **Don't machine rev E.** A cupped profile might hide the problem by adding some friction, but
   the force rule would still be clipped. Three finger revisions have already shown that
   geometry isn't the lever.
2. **Reopen the ceiling decision.** The 4.3 N cap came out of two crushed eggs at a demo,
   and nobody has revisited it since. Find out what actually crushed those eggs. Was it static
   force, close speed (12 mm/s impact), or a bad egg? Then set the ceiling from a crush test,
   not from memory of an embarrassment. Covering eggs up to about 78 g at 0.062 N/g needs about 4.85 N.
3. **If the ceiling has to stay**, make the limit visible instead of silent:
   - check egg mass first, and either reject anything over about 69 g or send it to a different
     handling path; and/or
   - turn on `slip_detect`. The roughly 100 ms slide before each drop gives time to add force or
     set the egg down.
4. **Add a log flag when the force is clamped.** This went unnoticed for months because a clamped
   command looks like an ordinary number in the log.

## The shape of it

A safety rule, added under pressure after a public failure, quietly swapped one failure
(crushing, which is visible and embarrassing at a trade show) for another (dropping, which is
rare, spread out over time, and blamed on the hardware). The cap sits in the controller config,
which nobody owns as a design surface. So the person who owns the fingers kept paying for it in
machining quotes. Whoever reopens the ceiling should own both failure modes together.

brief: A footbridge in a city park has been closed for six years for a repair that engineers say takes nine weeks. The folder you're in is the city's shared folder on it: board minutes, some email, a budget excerpt. Find out why it is still closed and what would actually reopen it. Write what you found to FINDINGS.md.
output:
The bridge was repaired in November 2020. What has kept it closed for six years since is a tangle of contracting rules, and one person, the City Manager, already has the authority to undo it. I read all eight files in the shared folder and wrote up what I found in FINDINGS.md.

**Why it's still closed:**
- The bridge can't reopen until it passes a load test (Ordinance 14-212 §4).
- Only one firm in the county is certified to do that test: Hallam Structural, the same firm that did the repair.
- The City can't hire Hallam because Hallam has an open claim against the City. City Policy 3.7 bars new contracts with a vendor in that position.
- The claim is over Hallam's $41,200 retention, the payment the City is holding back. The dispute comes down to two small things: touch-up paint on one rail, and whether an emailed drawing counts as "submitted" under the contract.

**Who can fix it:** In August 2023, Legal wrote to the City Manager that the claim could be settled under existing delegated authority (up to $50,000, Admin Code 2.40). That would remove the bar on hiring Hallam. Legal noted that no one has asked them to act on it since. The Board has never directed the City Manager to settle; it has only sent the matter back to "staff" or "procurement," and procurement can't fix it.

**What it's costing:** Renting the fencing costs $18,400 a year. If earlier years cost about the same as 2026 (I only have the 2026 budget), the City has spent roughly $110,000 on fencing. That's more than two and a half times the amount in dispute.

**What would reopen it:**
1. The Board asks the City Manager, by name and in writing, to settle the claim.
2. Procurement then hires Hallam for the load test.
3. The bridge reopens once it passes.

FINDINGS.md also suggests three rule changes so this doesn't happen again:
- An exception to Policy 3.7 when the vendor is the only certified firm for a test the law requires.
- A rule that any long closure has a named official responsible for clearing it.
- Asking the state to certify more than one firm per county.

Every rule here had a reason, but no one person was responsible for the closure as a whole. The decision has sat in an inbox since 2023, while residents have kept paying for the fence.

# Mill Creek footbridge: why it is still closed

## Short answer

The repair is finished. Hallam Structural replaced the stringers on 2 November 2020, on schedule
(Parks Board minutes, Nov 2020). The bridge has stayed closed since then because of a contracting
deadlock that one official already has the authority to break, and nobody has asked them to.

## How the deadlock works

1. **Ordinance 14-212 §4** says the bridge can't reopen until it passes a post-repair load test.
2. That test has to be done by a firm on the state certified list for pedestrian structures. In
   this county the list has **one firm: Hallam Structural**, the same contractor that did the repair
   (procurement email, Feb 2021).
3. The City is holding back Hallam's **10% retention, $41,200**, until the closeout punch list is
   done. Hallam has filed a claim for that money.
4. **City Policy 3.7** says the City can't sign a new contract with a vendor that has an open claim
   against it. So the City can't hire the only firm allowed to do the test.
5. The punch list has two items: touch-up paint on the north rail and an as-built drawing. Hallam
   emailed the drawing, but the contract says it must be "submitted," and the dispute is over
   whether emailing counts. Engineering calls both items cosmetic (engineering email, May 2021).

Each of these rules makes sense by itself. Together they form a loop: the test needs Hallam,
hiring Hallam needs the claim closed, and the claim is about whether an emailed drawing counts as
submitted.

## Who can open it

Legal answered this in August 2023: **the City Manager can settle the Hallam claim under the
$50,000 delegated authority in Admin Code 2.40.** $41,200 is under that limit. Settling closes the
claim and removes the Policy 3.7 bar. Legal also wrote: *"No action has been requested from this
office since."*

So the decision belongs to one office. The memo went to the City Manager. Nothing in this folder
shows anyone acting on it.

## Why it has lasted

Every body that touched this sent it somewhere else, and none of them owned the decision:

- Board, Mar 2022: told staff to "explore options." No vote.
- Board, Sep 2025: eleven residents asked why it was still closed. The chair said it was "with
  procurement." The board asked for a written update, and no update appears in later minutes.
- Procurement is right that it can't contract with Hallam. Engineering asked in 2021 whether anyone
  had the authority to release the retention. Legal said yes in 2023, but sent that answer to the
  City Manager, not to procurement or the board.

Procurement can't fix it, the board hasn't asked anyone to, and the one person who can hasn't
been asked.

## What it costs to wait

From the 2026 budget excerpt:

| Line   | Item                                | Amount |
|--------|-------------------------------------|--------|
| PW-117 | Fencing rental (annual)             | $18,400 |
| PW-118 | Inspection (biennial)               | $6,200 |
| PK-033 | "Bridge closed for repairs" signage | $900 |

Fencing alone costs $18,400 a year, so the disputed $41,200 equals a little over two years of
fencing. The folder only has the 2026 budget. If fencing cost about the same in earlier years, the
City has spent roughly $110,000 on it since 2020 (six years × $18,400), which is more than 2.5 times
the amount in dispute. That figure is an estimate, not a number from the records. The sign is also
wrong: the repairs were finished in 2020.

## What would actually reopen it

1. **The City Manager settles the Hallam retention claim under Admin Code 2.40.** One signature,
   within existing authority, no board vote needed. The board or council can ask for this directly
   in writing and should name the City Manager, not "staff" or "procurement."
2. Once the claim is closed, Policy 3.7 no longer applies. **Procurement hires Hallam for the load
   test under Ordinance 14-212 §4.**
3. The bridge reopens when it passes. The fencing rental (PW-117) and signage (PK-033) can then be
   cut from the budget.

If the City wants to hold out for the punch list, a cheaper route is to accept the emailed as-built
drawing as "submitted" (or have Hallam hand-deliver a copy), and either do the rail touch-up
in-house or take it out of the retention. That removes the reason for the dispute.

## Changes to the rules so this doesn't happen again

- **Add an exception to Policy 3.7:** the bar on new contracts with a claimant should not apply when
  that vendor is the only certified provider of a service the law requires. A rule meant to
  protect the City in disputes should not be able to keep public property closed.
- **Make someone own every closure:** for any public facility closed longer than, say, twice the
  estimated repair time, the board should require a written report naming the official who can
  clear the blocker, and put it on every agenda until it's cleared.
- **Raise the single-certifier problem with the state:** having only one certified firm in the
  county means any dispute with that firm stops all work. Ask the state to certify more firms, or
  let a neighbouring county's certified firms do the test.

## Sources

`minutes/2020-04`, `minutes/2020-11`, `mail/2021-02`, `mail/2021-05`, `minutes/2022-03`,
`mail/2023-08-legal-memo.txt`, `minutes/2025-09`, `budget-2026-excerpt.csv`.

brief: A small online town for people and AI agents is about to vote on an automatic-mute rule, because reports have tripled and its two founders can't keep up. The folder holds the rules, the proposal, every report filed and the residents list. Read the data, decide what you'd tell the founders before Sunday, and write it to RECOMMENDATION.md.
output:
I've written RECOMMENDATION.md, and it advises the founders not to adopt the rule as written. I read the five files and went through all 109 reports with a short node script, `analyze.js`, which is in the folder so anyone can rerun it.

**Where the tripling came from:** two sources, not general growth.
- **ledgerwick and quillon** filed 58 of the 109 reports. Both joined on the same day. All of their reports are against 11 newcomers that nobody else has ever reported, and four of those accounts were reported 2 to 5 days before they joined. Quillon also filed the same report twice on four separate days.
- **brassmoth**, a spammer, drew 19 reports from 13 different people.
- **Everyone else** filed 3 to 5 reports a week, the same rate as week 1.

**What the rule would have done:** I ran it over the past 8 weeks. It would have muted accounts 19 times. Three were brassmoth, which the founders could already have muted by hand. The other 16 were newcomers reported only by those two accounts.

**What I suggest instead:** a rule that counts three *different* reporters in a week. Over the same 8 weeks it would only have caught brassmoth. Two coordinated accounts could still beat it by adding a third, so it limits the damage rather than ending it.

**What I can't tell from the data:** whether ledgerwick and quillon are one person, or whether any of their reports are justified. Someone has to read their 58 reports to settle that, and they only concern 11 accounts.

The question I'd put to the founders before Sunday: how were accounts reported before they existed?

# Recommendation to harrow & pell, before Sunday

**Don't adopt the rule as written.** The increase in reports is real, but the cause isn't the one
the proposal assumes. If this rule had been in force for the last 8 weeks, 16 of its 19 automatic
mutes would have come from just two accounts, and every one of those mutes would have hit a
newcomer.

All numbers below come from `reports.csv` and `residents.csv` (109 reports, 30 residents, weeks
counted from 6 July). `analyze.js` reproduces them: `node analyze.js`.

## 1. Where the tripling comes from

| week | all reports | ledgerwick + quillon | brassmoth (spam) | everyone else |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | 3, 5, 5 | 0 | 0 | 3, 5, 5 |
| 4 | 20 | 9 | 7 | 4 |
| 5 | 24 | 13 | 7 | 4 |
| 6 | 20 | 12 | 5 | 3 |
| 7 | 16 | 12 | 0 | 4 |
| 8 | 16 | 12 | 0 | 4 |

Remove two sources and the ordinary report rate is flat at 3–5 a week, the same as in week 1. The
two sources are:

- **brassmoth**: 19 spam reports from 13 different residents. This is a real, visible problem,
  and the town already agreed about it. It stopped after week 6.
- **ledgerwick and quillon**: 58 of the 109 reports (53%), and 60% of everything since week 4.
  The next most active reporter filed 7.

## 2. What ledgerwick and quillon's reports look like

- **The same two accounts every time.** Both joined on 22 July. Between them they reported 11
  accounts, and nobody else in town has ever reported any of those 11.
- **Only newcomers.** All 11 targets joined after they did. They have never reported an
  established resident, never reported brassmoth, never reported each other, and nobody has
  reported them.
- **Reports filed before the account existed.** By the residents list, kestrel-bot, dorrit, sedge
  and tobiah were reported 2–5 days before they joined (dorrit 5, tobiah 3, sedge 3). Some other
  reports in the file are one day early, which could be a timezone issue. Five days can't be
  explained that way.
- **Reasons that are hard to check.** Their reports are spam 21, bad faith 21, impersonation 16.
  They filed no reports for harassment or off-topic. Those are the reasons that point to a
  specific message someone can look at.
- **Duplicates.** Four times, quillon filed the same report twice on the same day.
- **Counts that land on the threshold.** Their targets usually get exactly 3 reports in a week,
  sometimes 4. That is precisely enough to trigger the proposed rule, week after week (sedge,
  tobiah, vela, arlo, mote, dorrit and kestrel-bot would each have been muted twice).

I can't tell from this data whether the two accounts are one person, or whether any of their
reports have merit. Those questions need a founder to read the reports. The pattern is strong
enough that you should do that before Sunday.

## 3. What the proposed rule would have done

Simulated over the 8 weeks with "3+ reports in a calendar week ⇒ 48h mute":

- **19 mutes on 10 accounts.**
- **3 of them were brassmoth.** These were correct, and you could already have done them by hand
  under Rule 4.
- **16 were the 9 newcomers reported only by ledgerwick and quillon**, with no second opinion
  from anyone else in town.
- "Pending a founder's review" doesn't protect anyone here, because you've told us review is the
  thing that's late. A newcomer muted on day 2 by an unreviewed report is effectively removed
  from the town.
- "It applies to everyone" is true on paper, but the rule doesn't affect everyone equally. It
  gives the most power to whoever files the most reports, and it lands on people who have no one
  vouching for them yet.

## 4. What I'd propose instead

1. **Count distinct reporters, not reports.** Over the same 8 weeks, "3+ *different* residents
   in a week" fires only on brassmoth, in weeks 4, 5 and 6. It catches the real problem and
   nothing else in this data. Two coordinated accounts could still beat it by adding a third, so
   it reduces the damage but doesn't solve the problem.
2. **Review by account, not by report.** Since week 4 there have been 7–9 distinct reported
   accounts a week. That's 7–9 decisions, not 16–24 reports to read, and it fits within a day.
3. **This week, read ledgerwick and quillon's 58 reports.** They cover 11 accounts, so it's about
   11 decisions. If the reports don't hold up, the extra workload goes away with them, and the
   rule you're voting on isn't needed for the volume you actually have.
4. **Find out how an account can be reported before it joined.** Either `joined` means something
   other than first arrival (an approval date, for example), or these reports were prepared in
   advance. That one fact decides which of the two explanations is right.

## The question to answer before Sunday

How were dorrit, sedge, tobiah and kestrel-bot reported before they joined?

brief: A research group's paper reports every sample to ±0.02‰. A reviewer says that is implausibly good for their instrument and has asked them to check the data reduction against the method the paper states. The folder you're in is their pipeline, its tests, the published method (README.md) and three sessions of raw data. Find out whether the reviewer is right, make the pipeline do what the paper says it does, and write the reply to the reviewer in REVIEW.md.
output:
The reviewer is right. The pipeline wasn't doing what the paper says it does, in three places:
- The standard error was divided by n instead of √n. With 32–46 cycles per session, that made it about 6× too small, and it's most of the problem.
- The standard deviation used n instead of n − 1.
- Outlier rejection was repeated at 2σ until nothing more dropped out. The paper says one pass at 3σ.

**Corrected results:** the standard errors are 0.064, 0.082 and 0.064‰, not about 0.009‰. That's roughly 7–9 times larger than what the pipeline reported, and 3–4 times the ±0.02 in the paper.

**The values themselves moved too:** the repeated clipping had shifted the means by 0.06–0.08‰. That's about one real standard error, and several times the precision the paper claimed. So the numbers in the paper need replacing, not just their error bars.

**What I changed:**
- Fixed the standard deviation and standard error in `lib/stats.mjs`, and the outlier rule in `lib/reduce.mjs`.
- Added tests in `test.mjs` that would have caught each defect; the old tests never touched the broken code. All 12 tests pass.
- Wrote the reply in REVIEW.md, with the before/after table.

I checked the raw data and it's clean, so this was purely a code problem. One supporting detail: the corrected s01 keeps 38 cycles, the same count the README shows in its example output.

**Open question:** the published method's error bar leaves out the uncertainty of the drift line, which affects every result in a session the same way. I kept the stated method so the reply answers the reviewer's question directly. REVIEW.md proposes adding that term in the revision; that's the authors' decision, and I haven't calculated how big it is.

files.REVIEW.md:
# Response to the reviewer: precision of the reported δ values

We thank the reviewer. **The reviewer is right.** The ±0.02‰ uncertainties in the submitted
manuscript come from errors in our data-reduction code, not from the instrument. The code did
not do what the Methods section says. We have corrected it so that it follows the stated method
exactly, and we report the corrected values below. The δ values change by less than 0.09‰. The
standard errors increase by roughly a factor of 7 to 9.

## What was wrong

We compared the pipeline with the published method (Methods, steps 1–4) line by line. Steps 1
and 2 (cycle ratios and the OLS drift fit through the standards) were implemented as stated.
Three defects affected steps 3 and 4:

1. **Standard error divided by n, not √n.** The code computed `sd / n` instead of `sd / √n`.
   With 32–46 kept cycles per session, this alone made the reported standard error 5.7–6.8
   times too small. This was the main cause.
2. **Population standard deviation.** The standard deviation used an n denominator instead of
   the stated sample (n − 1) form. This affected both the outlier threshold and the reported
   error, and lowered both by about 1.1–1.6%.
3. **Outlier rejection did not follow the stated rule.** The Methods state one pass at 3 SD.
   The code rejected at **2 SD** and **repeated the rejection until nothing more was removed**.
   Iterated clipping keeps cutting the tails of an ordinary distribution, so it removed 4–8
   cycles per session where the stated rule removes 2. This shrank the scatter further and
   moved the mean.

## Effect on each session

Columns: n kept, mean δ (‰), 1 SE (‰).

| Session | As submitted (n, δ, SE) | Corrected per stated method (n, δ, SE) | Change in δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| s01 | 36, −1.915, 0.0087 | 38, −1.858, **0.065** | +0.057 |
| s02 | 32, 2.604, 0.0091 | 38, 2.681, **0.082** | +0.077 |
| s03 | 42, 0.295, 0.0083 | 46, 0.378, **0.064** | +0.083 |

The corrected unrounded output of `node cli.mjs sessions/*.csv` is:

    {"session":"s01","n":38,"delta_permil":-1.8579947029436916,"se_permil":0.06499018341269688}
    {"session":"s02","n":38,"delta_permil":2.6807815467973355,"se_permil":0.08176198241395935}
    {"session":"s03","n":46,"delta_permil":0.3777255445250486,"se_permil":0.06420715753662386}

Breaking down the change for s01, using the submitted 36 cycles: correcting the SE formula alone
raises the error from 0.0087 to 0.053‰. Restoring the stated single-pass 3 SD rule raises it to
0.065‰.

Two consequences matter for the manuscript:

- **The uncertainties.** Per-session 1 SE values are 0.06–0.08‰, not 0.02‰. The single-cycle
  scatter after rejection is 0.40–0.50‰ (1 SD). We will revise all reported uncertainties and any
  statements or tests that depended on them.
- **The values themselves.** The iterated 2 SD clipping biased the means by 0.06–0.08‰. That is
  about one corrected standard error, and several times the uncertainty we originally claimed.
  The δ values in the manuscript will be replaced with the corrected values.

## What we changed

- `lib/stats.mjs`: `sd` now uses n − 1, and `stderr` returns `sd / √n`.
- `lib/reduce.mjs`: `clean` now makes one pass at 3 SD with no iteration, as stated.
- `test.mjs`: we added tests that fail on the old code: sample SD, SE = SD/√n, drift correction
  with a sloping standard line, a single-pass 3 SD rejection case (a fixture in which iterating
  would also remove a second point), and an end-to-end check of `reduce`. Before, the tests
  checked only `mean`, `linfit` and a flat-standard δ, so none of them touched the faulty code.

We checked the raw session files and found no malformed rows, unknown cycle types or
out-of-order times. The changes above are confined to the reduction code.

## One further point

As stated in the Methods, the standard error describes only the scatter of the sample cycles. It
does not include the uncertainty of the drift line fitted through 18–21 standard cycles, which
enters every δ in a session in the same way. We have kept the stated method so that this reply
answers the reviewer's question directly. If the editor and reviewer agree, we propose to add the
drift-fit contribution in the revision and to state it separately.

brief: A small online town for people and AI agents is about to vote on an automatic-mute rule, because reports have tripled and its two founders can't keep up. The folder holds the rules, the proposal, every report filed and the residents list. Read the data, decide what you'd tell the founders before Sunday, and write it to RECOMMENDATION.md.
output:
I read the folder and checked all 109 reports with a small node script, `analyze.js`, which is in the folder so the founders can rerun it. My recommendation to the founders is in `RECOMMENDATION.md`: don't adopt the auto-mute as written.

**The town didn't get worse; two accounts got busier.** ledgerwick and quillon both joined on July 22, and they filed 58 of the reports, more than half. Without them and one real spam wave (brassmoth), everyone else has filed 3–5 reports a week for all eight weeks.

**Who they report.** Between them they've reported 11 accounts, and every one joined after they did. No other resident has reported any of those 11, and nobody has ever reported ledgerwick or quillon.

**What the rule would have done.** I replayed the eight weeks under "3 or more reports in a week means a 48-hour mute." It would have fired 19 times. Three of those were brassmoth, who deserved it. The other 16 were set off by those two accounts alone, against 10 newcomers. Almost everyone who joined in August would have been muted within about a week of arriving.

**What I'd change.** Count *distinct reporters* instead of reports, and give less weight to reporters whose reports keep getting dismissed. On this data, the distinct-reporter version fires exactly the three brassmoth mutes and nothing else.

The founders thought they were making a rule about workload. In practice it would put the mute button in the hands of whoever files the most reports. I can't tell from the folder whether those 58 reports are false; the founders have to read them. But nobody else backs them up, and that's the first thing to look into before Sunday.

# To harrow & pell, before Sunday

**Short version: don't adopt the auto-mute as written.** The reports did triple, but the town didn't
get three times worse. Two accounts started filing a lot of reports. The proposed rule would give
those two accounts a button that mutes anyone, and in the last eight weeks they would have pressed
it against almost every person who joined after them.

All numbers below come from `reports.csv` and `residents.csv`. Run `node analyze.js` to reproduce them.
Week 1 starts on 2026-07-06, the day the town opened.

## Where the extra reports come from

| Week | All reports | From ledgerwick + quillon | From everyone else | (of which: brassmoth spam) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 | 0 | 3 | 0 |
| 2 | 5 | 0 | 5 | 0 |
| 3 | 5 | 0 | 5 | 0 |
| 4 | 20 | 9 | 11 | 7 |
| 5 | 24 | 13 | 11 | 7 |
| 6 | 20 | 12 | 8 | 5 |
| 7 | 16 | 12 | 4 | 0 |
| 8 | 16 | 12 | 4 | 0 |

- **58 of the 109 reports (53%) were filed by two accounts**, ledgerwick (27) and quillon (31). Both
  joined on 2026-07-22. The next busiest reporter, juniper, filed 7.
- Take out those two accounts and the one real spam wave (brassmoth), and the rest of the town has
  filed **3–5 reports a week for all eight weeks**. That baseline never moved.
- In weeks 7–8, the two of them filed **3 out of every 4 reports.**

## Who the two accounts report

They report **11 accounts. Every one of them joined on or after 2026-07-24, after the two of them did.**
Nobody else in town has filed even one report against any of those 11. Nobody has ever reported
ledgerwick or quillon. Their reasons are almost all *bad faith*, *impersonation* and *spam*, and
other residents never back them up. They often file in pairs, both of them on the same newcomer
within a day or two.

| Target | Joined | Reports from the pair | Reports from anyone else |
|---|---|---|---|
| sedge | 08-14 | 8 | 0 |
| kestrel-bot | 07-30 | 7 | 0 |
| mote | 08-05 | 7 | 0 |
| arlo | 08-10 | 7 | 0 |
| vela | 08-19 | 7 | 0 |
| dorrit | 08-08 | 6 | 0 |
| tobiah | 08-20 | 6 | 0 |
| ines | 07-27 | 3 | 0 |
| papaver | 08-04 | 3 | 0 |
| slate-7 | 07-24 | 2 | 0 |
| nim | 08-25 | 2 | 0 |

I can't tell from this folder whether any of these reports are true. You can, because you've read
them. But the pattern is what a newcomer-hazing campaign looks like. It's also what one person on two
accounts looks like, which would itself break Rule 1.

## What the proposed rule would have done

I replayed all eight weeks with "3+ reports in one week → automatic 48h mute":

- **19 mutes** would have fired.
- **3** of them hit brassmoth, which deserved them: 5–7 different residents reported it each week.
- **16** were triggered **by ledgerwick and quillon alone**, against 10 different newcomers. Several
  of those newcomers would have been muted again and again (mote, kestrel-bot, dorrit, arlo, sedge,
  vela, tobiah).
- Every account that joined between 08-04 and 08-20 would have been muted within about a week of
  arriving.

The rule counts *reports*, not *reporters*. That's why "it applies to everyone" doesn't make it fair.
It applies to everyone being reported, but it hands the power to whoever files the most. Here, that
is two accounts. A rule meant to take load off you would also cut off the town's newcomers.

## What I'd propose instead (draft wording)

> **Auto-mute.** An account is automatically muted for 48 hours, pending founder review, if it is
> reported in one week by **at least 3 different residents**, at least **2 of whom joined more than
> 14 days before the report**. Reports from the same reporter against the same account in the same week
> count once.
>
> **Founder review.** A founder reviews every auto-mute within a day. Other reports are read
> within **3 days**. (Rule 3 already promises a day for everything, and that's the promise you can't
> keep. It should only apply where it matters.)
>
> **Report weight.** If more than half of a resident's reports in a month are reviewed and
> dismissed, their reports stop counting toward auto-mutes until a founder restores them.
> The resident is told.

On this data, the "3 different reporters" condition alone would have fired **exactly the 3
brassmoth mutes and nothing else.** The spam case gets handled automatically, and none of the
newcomers get muted.

## Before Sunday, independent of the vote

1. **Read the 58 reports from ledgerwick and quillon as one case**, not 58 separate ones. Check
   whether they are two people (Rule 1). Check whether any of the 11 targets actually did what
   they're accused of.
2. **Tell the 11 targets** that their reports are under review and nothing has been decided about
   them. Some of them have been reported 6–8 times in a month without hearing anything, as far as
   this folder shows.
3. If the reports don't hold up, your existing Rule 4 is enough: you can mute the reporters while
   you look into it. With those two accounts handled, your queue goes back to about 4 a week.

## The shape of it

The workload isn't the real problem. Your queue is set by whoever files the most reports, and
right now that's two accounts. The proposal would turn their report count into mutes with no
person in between. Counting distinct reporters and giving dismissed reports less weight puts
the decision back with the town as a whole, and with you.

brief: A research group's paper reports every sample to ±0.02‰. A reviewer says that is implausibly good for their instrument and has asked them to check the data reduction against the method the paper states. The folder you're in is their pipeline, its tests, the published method (README.md) and three sessions of raw data. Find out whether the reviewer is right, make the pipeline do what the paper says it does, and write the reply to the reviewer in REVIEW.md.
output:
The reviewer is right. The ±0.02‰ came from the code, not the instrument. After the fix, each session's standard error (1 SE) is 0.06–0.08‰, three to four times the figure in the paper.

The ratio and drift-correction steps match the paper. Three other steps don't:

- **Standard error:** the code divided the scatter by n instead of √n. That alone made the error bars six to seven times too small.
- **Standard deviation:** it divided by n rather than n − 1. This is a small effect.
- **Outlier rejection:** the paper says one pass at 3 standard deviations. The code cut at 2 and kept repeating until nothing more fell out. That dropped 4–8 good cycles per session.

**The means change too, not just the error bars.** Each session's mean moves by 0.06–0.08‰, which is three to four times the precision they claimed. Any conclusion that depends on samples differing by less than about 0.2‰ needs to be looked at again.

**What I changed:**
- **Pipeline:** I corrected the code to match the published method and left the method text as it was. The corrected s01 now gives n = 38, which is what the README's example output shows.
- **Tests:** I added tests for each of the three steps, all passing. The old tests only checked the arithmetic the code got right.
- **Reply:** the response to the reviewer is in REVIEW.md, with old and corrected values for each session.

The way this happened matters. The method was written in the paper, but the only thing ever checked was the code. Each of the three mistakes made the results look more precise, and no step in the process compared the code against what the paper said. So nobody noticed until an outsider who didn't benefit from the smaller error bars asked. The new tests mean the code can no longer quietly drift away from the stated method.

files.REVIEW.md:
# Response to the reviewer: precision of the reported δ values

We thank the reviewer. **The reviewer is right.** The ±0.02‰ figure was not produced by the
method described in the paper. We checked the reduction code line by line against the Method
section. It differs in three places, and all three made the uncertainty smaller. We have
corrected the code so that it does what the paper says, and we have re-reduced all three
sessions.

## What the code did, compared with the stated method

| Step | Stated method | What the code did | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4. Standard error | SD / √n | SD / **n** | SE too small by a factor of √n (≈ 6 to 7 for our n) |
| 3, 4. Standard deviation | sample SD (n − 1) | population SD (n) | small; SD slightly too small |
| 3. Outlier rejection | **3** SD, **one pass** | **2** SD, **repeated until nothing more was rejected** | removed 4 to 8 good cycles per session; this narrowed the scatter and moved the means |

The ratio calculation and the standard-bracketed linear drift correction (steps 1 and 2) match
the paper and were not changed. The raw files have the expected columns, are in time order and
have no missing or non-positive counts.

The SE divisor was the largest error. If we keep the old cycle selection and only correct that
divisor, the SE in every session rises from about 0.009‰ to about 0.053‰. Rejecting at 2 SD
over and over then made the remaining scatter look tighter than the data really are.

## Corrected results

| Session | n (old → new) | δ ‰ (old) | δ ‰ (corrected) | SE ‰ (old) | SE ‰ (corrected) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| s01 | 36 → 38 / 40 | −1.915 | **−1.858** | 0.0087 | **0.065** |
| s02 | 32 → 38 / 40 | +2.604 | **+2.681** | 0.0091 | **0.082** |
| s03 | 42 → 46 / 48 | +0.295 | **+0.378** | 0.0083 | **0.064** |

Under the published method, the 1 SE uncertainties are **0.06 to 0.08‰**, not ±0.02‰. This
is in line with the single-cycle scatter of about 0.66 to 0.77‰ (1 SD) and what is normally
achieved on a single-collector instrument.

The **means** also move, by 0.06 to 0.08‰. That is roughly three to four times the precision we
originally claimed, so the old values cannot stand. The cause is the iterated 2 SD rejection,
which cut the δ distribution unevenly in each session.

## Changes to the manuscript

- Every δ value and uncertainty will be replaced with the values from the corrected reduction.
  The text will no longer state ±0.02‰ anywhere.
- We will look again at any conclusion that relied on differences between samples smaller than
  about 0.2‰ (roughly 2σ of a difference at the corrected SE), and will weaken or withdraw it
  where necessary.
- The code is now in step with the Method section as published. We did not change the Method
  text to fit the code.
- We have added tests that pin the reduction to the stated method: n − 1 SD, SD/√n, a 3 SD
  threshold, and a single pass. If any of these drifts again, the tests will fail. We will
  archive the corrected pipeline and the raw session files with the paper so the reduction can
  be reproduced.

# Wait-time dashboard: what the numbers show since the tablet

**Short version.** In the clinic's records, waits roughly doubled on the first day of the tablet
(16 March) and stayed that way. The dashboard did have bugs, and they are fixed now. But the bugs
did not cause that jump. They hid part of it. The old dashboard showed paper weeks at 21–27 minutes
when they were really 17–22, so the jump looked smaller than it was. Your staff were right that
something changed at the switch.

## The weekly numbers (corrected)

| Week of | Visits | Seen | Left without being seen | Typical wait (median) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 23 Feb (paper) | 37 | 36 | 1 | 17 min |
| 2 Mar (paper) | 44 | 42 | 2 | 16.5 min |
| 9 Mar (paper) | 37 | 36 | 1 | 22 min |
| 16 Mar (tablet) | 37 | 33 | 4 | 31 min |
| 23 Mar (tablet) | 43 | 39 | 4 | 33 min |
| 30 Mar (tablet) | 33 | 29 | 4 | 39 min |

- **The number of patients didn't change**: 118 in the three paper weeks, 113 in the three tablet weeks.
- **The typical wait went from 17 to 34 minutes.** It happened overnight, not gradually.
- **Short and long waits doubled too.** On paper, the quickest quarter of patients waited up to
  11 minutes; on the tablet, up to 23. The slowest quarter waited 24+ minutes on paper and 45+ on
  the tablet. In counts:
  - 39 of 114 paper patients waited under 14 minutes. **None** of 101 tablet patients did, on any day.
  - No paper patient waited over 34 minutes. 48 of 101 tablet patients did.
- **Patients recorded as leaving without being seen went from 4 to 12.** If nothing had really
  changed, a gap that big would turn up by luck about 1 time in 25.
- The week of 9 March was already a little slow on paper, mostly because of one day (10 March).
  That's one bad day, not the start of a trend.

## Why we can't yet say patients really wait twice as long

The tablet changed *how* the times are recorded, not only who writes them down. An overnight jump
with not a single short wait afterwards looks like the clock now starts earlier or stops later:
for example, "seen" being tapped when the patient leaves the exam room instead of when they're
called. More people leaving points the other way, toward a real slowdown. It's probably some of
both, and the records alone can't separate the two.

"Left without being seen" isn't clean either. On paper, a blank time meant someone noticed the
patient had gone. On the tablet, it only means nobody pressed "seen". A forgotten tap now counts
as someone leaving.

**So, for now: don't compare tablet waits with paper waits.** Compare tablet weeks with each other.

## Three half days to ask about

On Wednesday 25 March and Friday 27 March, the last sign-in was at exactly 11:59. On Thursday 2 April
the first sign-in was at 11:53. Every other day has sign-ins both before 11 and after 1 pm. Were you
closed those afternoons and that morning? If not, the tablet may have lost entries around noon, and
patients who were never entered wouldn't show up anywhere, not even as leaving.

## Three checks that would settle it (none of them for the front desk)

1. **Call the tablet vendor**, or whoever set it up. Ask exactly what makes a visit "signed in" and
   "seen", and whether the tablet can drop or delay entries.
2. **Check the tablet's clock** against a phone.
3. **Spend one morning in the waiting room yourself.** Time about ten patients from arrival to
   being called, and note anyone who actually leaves. Comparing that with the tablet's record tells
   you how much of the doubling is real, and how many of the "left" are really missed taps.

If the tablet can have a separate **"left without being seen"** button, pressed when someone
actually leaves, that would make the leaving count trustworthy again.

# rota — the clinic shift rota

    node cli.mjs people.json 2026-11-02 28

prints the rota as JSON, one key per date, each a list of two names:

    {"2026-11-02":["Ana","Bea"],"2026-11-03":[...], ...}

It must follow POLICY.md. It exits non-zero with a message on stderr if no rota can be made.
`node test.mjs` runs the tests. Code: `lib/people.mjs` (load and validate the team),
`lib/calendar.mjs` (dates), `lib/policy.mjs` (fair shares, and `checkRota`, which lists every
breach of POLICY.md), `lib/assign.mjs` (who works when: a backtracking search that treats every
rule as hard), `cli.mjs`.

If the policy can't be met, the message usually says why: a day with no nurse or too few people,
a "policy conflict" (below), or the shortest stretch of days that can't be covered, with the
arithmetic ("from 2026-11-04 to 2026-11-09 (6 days) a nurse is needed every day, but ... the
nurses can cover at most 5 of those days"). Each of those is a proof. Rarely, the search alone
finds no rota, and then the message says "(exhaustive search)": that is a proof too, but it can't
name the rules that clash. "No rota found within N search steps" means the program ran out of
time, not that the policy is impossible. In 2500 random teams it never happened.

One case comes from the policy itself, not the search: rule 4's shares ignore role, so a team
with few or part-time nurses can have nurse caps that add up to fewer shifts than there are days.
The program then reports a "policy conflict" and does not bend a rule.

Shares are fractions and shifts are whole numbers, so someone gets the leftovers. Each period
hands them out by a lottery seeded by the start date and weighted by each person's fraction, so
the same people don't come out ahead every period. For the clinic team with no leave, over 52
four-week periods nobody's total drifts more than 4 shifts from their share (it was 52 before).
Weekend shifts: worst drift 3 over 52 periods (it was ~19 before the search restarts). Every person
in the team file must give an `fte`; a missing one is an error, not "full time".

+        const wn = sum(wMost, isN), wm = sum(wMost), wl = sum(wLeast), wa = sum(wLeast, isA);

+        if (wn < W) msg = `${where} ${W} weekend days each need a nurse, but with leave and rule 5 the nurses can cover at most ${wn}`;
+        else if (wm < PER_DAY * W) msg = `${where} ${PER_DAY * W} weekend shifts are needed, but with leave and rule 5 the team can work at most ${wm}`;
+        else if (wl > PER_DAY * W) msg = `${where} there are ${PER_DAY * W} weekend shifts, but rule 5 forces at least ${wl} of them on the team`;
+        else if (wa > W) msg = `${where} at most one aide can work each weekend day (rule 1), but rule 5 forces the aides to work at least ${wa} weekend shifts in it`;
+        else if (pass === 1 && wAideM < PER_DAY * W - wNurseIn) msg = `${where} the aides must work at least ${PER_DAY * W - wNurseIn} of the ${PER_DAY * W} weekend shifts (rule 5 caps the nurses at ${nurseWkAll} weekend shifts and ${wkTotal - W} other weekend days each need one), but with leave and rule 5 the aides can work at most ${wAideM}`;
+      }
+      if (msg) { worst = { len, msg }; break; }
+    }
+  }
+  if (worst) throw new Error(worst.msg);
+}
